title: Is Worry Associated With Social Exclusion in School? Within‐Person Relations From Age 10 to 16
abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction The need‐to‐belong theory stipulates that social exclusion should influence cognitive processing. However, no longitudinal studies have examined its effects on cognitive processing (e.g., worry) associated with internalizing problems. In this study, we investigated whether social exclusion in school predicts worry from childhood to adolescence, and whether these associations differ by gender. Methods The sample consisted of 655 Norwegian 10‐year‐olds who were assessed biennially from age 10 to 16 between 2013/2014 and 2020/2021. Assessments included teacher‐reported data on social exclusion in school and self‐reported levels of worry. To examine prospective within‐person effects of social exclusion in school on worry, a random intercept cross‐lagged panel model (RICLPM) was utilized. Results Results showed that worry increased with age, whereas social exclusion in school did not. RI‐CLPM revealed that increased social exclusion in school at age 12 predicted increased worry at age 14, but only for girls. No gender differences were observed in the levels of social exclusion in school, suggesting higher reactivity to social exclusion in girls. Conclusions The study extends partial support for the need‐to‐belong theory in a real‐world context, during an important developmental transition in children's lives.
